title: Moments and Centers of Mass
lead: The center of mass of a system is its balance point, its moment divided by its total mass: first for point masses on a line and in the plane, then, cutting a lamina into rectangles, as integrals for the centroid of a region. Symmetry places some centroids without integrating, and the theorem of Pappus turns a centroid into the volume of a solid of revolution.
objectives: Find the center of mass of objects distributed along a line.
Locate the center of mass of a thin plate.
Use symmetry to help locate the centroid of a thin plate.
Apply the theorem of Pappus for volume.
summary_html:
• Mathematically, the center of mass of a system is the point at which the total mass of the system could be concentrated without changing the moment. Loosely speaking, the center of mass can be thought of as the balancing point of the system.
  • For point masses distributed along a number line, the moment of the system with respect to the origin is $\kM=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\km_{i}x_{i}.$ For point masses distributed in a plane, the moments of the system with respect to the x- and y-axes, respectively, are $\kMx=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\km_{i}y_{i}$ and $\kMy=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\km_{i}x_{i},$ respectively.
  • For a lamina bounded above by a function $\kf(x),$ the moments of the system with respect to the x- and y-axes, respectively, are $\kMx=\krho\int_a^{b}\frac{{[\kf(x)]}^{2}}{2}dx$ and $\kMy=\krho\int_a^{b}x\kf(x)dx.$
  • The x- and y-coordinates of the center of mass can be found by dividing the moments around the y-axis and around the x-axis, respectively, by the total mass. The symmetry principle says that if a region is symmetric with respect to a line, then the centroid of the region lies on the line.
  • The theorem of Pappus for volume says that if a region is revolved around an external axis, the volume of the resulting solid is equal to the area of the region multiplied by the distance traveled by the centroid of the region.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose four point masses are placed on a number line as follows:

$$\begin{array}{llll}m_{1}=12\;\text{kg,}\;\text{placed at}\;x_{1}=-4\;\text{m} & & & m_{2}=12\;\text{kg,}\;\text{placed at}\;x_{2}=4\;\text{m} \\ m_{3}=30\;\text{kg,}\;\text{placed at}\;x_{3}=2\;\text{m} & & & m_{4}=6\;\text{kg,}\;\text{placed at}\;x_{4}=-6\;\text{m}.\end{array}$$

Find the moment of the system with respect to the origin and find the center of mass of the system.

parts.hint: Use the process from the previous example.

exercises.prompt: Let R be the region bounded above by the graph of the function $f(x)=x^{2}$ and below by the x-axis over the interval $[0,2].$ Find the centroid of the region.

answer.solution: The centroid of the region is $(3/2,6/5).$

For the following exercises, use the theorem of Pappus to determine the volume of the shape.

A general cone created by rotating a triangle with vertices $(0,0),$ $(a,0),$ and $(0,b)$ around the $y$-axis. Does your answer agree with the volume of a cone?

answer.solution: The triangle has area $A=\frac{ab}{2}$ and, at the average of its vertices, its centroid at $\left(\frac{a}{3},\frac{b}{3}\right).$ Turned about the y-axis, the centroid travels $d=2\pi\cdot\frac{a}{3},$ so $V=A d=\frac{ab}{2}\cdot\frac{2\pi a}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\pi a^{2}b,$ the volume of a cone of radius a and height b.

For the following exercises, use the theorem of Pappus to determine the volume of the shape.

A sphere created by rotating a semicircle with radius $a$ around the $y$-axis. Does your answer agree with the volume of a sphere?

answer.solution: Take the half-disk of radius a to the right of the y-axis. Its area is $A=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{2},$ and it lies between $f(x)=\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ and $g(x)=-\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}$ on $[0,a],$ so with $\rho=1$ its moment about the y-axis is $M_{y}=\int_{0}^{a}2x\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx=\frac{2a^{3}}{3}$ and its centroid is at $\bar{x}=\frac{2a^{3}/3}{\pi a^{2}/2}=\frac{4a}{3\pi}.$ The centroid travels $d=2\pi\cdot\frac{4a}{3\pi}=\frac{8a}{3},$ so $V=\frac{\pi a^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{8a}{3}=\frac{4}{3}\pi a^{3},$ the volume of a sphere.

assumes.text: The masses balance each other if and only if $\km_{1}d_{1}=\km_{2}d_{2}.$
With the fulcrum at $\kxbar,$ the distances to the masses are $d_{1}=|\kxbar-x_{1}|$ and $d_{2}=|x_{2}-\kxbar|.$
The fulcrum lies between the masses: $x_{1}\le \kxbar\le x_{2}.$

assumes.text: The mass of the rectangle is its area multiplied by the constant density $\krho,$ that is, $\krho \kf(x_i^{*})\Delta x.$

then.why: Adding the masses of all the rectangles approximates the mass of the lamina.

steps.cap: This is a Riemann sum, so we take the limit as $n\to \infty.$

assumes.text: Treating the rectangle as a point mass at its center of mass $(x_i^{*},(\kf(x_i^{*}))/2)$ does not change the moment.
The moment with respect to the $x$-axis is the mass multiplied by the distance to the $x$-axis.
The mass of the rectangle is its area multiplied by the constant density $\krho,$ that is, $\krho \kf(x_i^{*})\Delta x.$

then.why: The moment of each rectangle is its mass multiplied by the distance from its center of mass to the $x$-axis.

steps.cap: Adding the moments of the rectangles gives a Riemann sum, and we take its limit as $n\to \infty.$
